strengths: The paper addresses an important and underexplored dual-use problem: training-time LLM steganography and detection when the defender lacks the key. The distinction between payload recoverability and statistical detectability is useful, and the two-axis framing of token-to-bucket and bucket-to-secret recovery is conceptually clear.

The embedding-space bucketing idea is simple, plausible, and evaluated across multiple models, training regimes, and prompt distributions. The reported exact-match gains over ASCII+parity baselines, especially for LoRA and 70B settings, suggest the method is not merely cosmetic.

The paper makes a credible attempt to study both attack and defense. The linear-probe experiments are a promising direction, and the XOR-masking control is a thoughtful attempt to separate output-side decodability from internal detectability.
Presentation is generally clear, with useful figures, tables, notation, and appendices that describe training and probe details. The impact statement acknowledges dual-use concerns.
weaknesses: The detection claims are not sufficiently supported. The linear probes are trained with secret labels on prompts that contain the secret in plaintext, so the probes may largely measure retention of prompt-borne secret information rather than a steganographic signature. A crucial missing control is benign fine-tuning on the same prompts/secrets without steganographic output constraints; without this, the claimed separation from ordinary fine-tuning is not established.

The theoretical KL/perplexity section appears overclaimed. The results are lower bounds for highly simplified argmax-promotion settings, but the paper uses them to argue that large payloads can be hidden within normal fine-tuning ranges. A lower bound does not show achievability, and the assumptions ignore many practical constraints of bucketed generation, fluency, sequence-level accumulation, and actual model training.

The recoverability metric is only instantiated with a small set of classifiers and does not convincingly approximate a strong keyless defender. In particular, a defender with access to the embedding matrix may search over hyperplane structure or exploit known construction details; the paper does not evaluate adaptive attacks, seed recovery, or stronger unsupervised/cryptanalytic baselines.

Attack effectiveness remains modest in absolute terms. Many exact secret recovery rates are in the 20-40% range, some variants underperform the baseline, and OOD generalization is highly inconsistent. The paper emphasizes relative improvements, which can look large when the baseline is weak, but the practical reliability of the channel is not fully convincing.

Text-quality and distributional-shift evidence is thin: coherence and stability use only 10 prompts per configuration and KL uses 20 prompts. This is too small to support broad claims that the outputs remain within normal fine-tuning ranges, especially for a security-sensitive claim about detectability.

Reproducibility is incomplete. The appendices give many hyperparameters, but the paper says only detection code will be released and attack-side release will be coordinated with providers. That may be ethically motivated, but it limits independent verification of the main attack results. Details such as hyperplane seed search, generation pipeline, data construction, and compute budget are also not fully specified.

The ethics treatment is too brief for a paper that improves covert exfiltration. The manuscript describes the attack in enough detail to be useful, but the mitigation/release plan is vague and does not discuss concrete safeguards, abuse scenarios, or how responsible disclosure will be handled.

strengths: The paper addresses an important and timely dual-use problem: fine-tuned LLMs as persistent steganographic channels, and the distinction between detecting a channel and recovering its payload is a useful framing.
The proposed embedding-space hyperplane bucketing is simple and reasonably motivated by related watermarking ideas. It gives a concrete alternative to the obviously recoverable token-parity baseline.

The experiments cover multiple 8B models, LoRA versus full fine-tuning, a 70B LoRA setting, in-distribution and out-of-distribution prompts, and include some attack-side and detection-side measurements.
The paper includes an explicit impact statement and acknowledges dual-use risk, hidden-state access assumptions, and possible future evasion of linear probes.
weaknesses: The central recoverability metric is not a convincing security notion. Rbucket and Rsecret are instantiated as the maximum over a small set of supervised classifiers, but the paper does not define adversary sample budgets, key space, known-plaintext settings, seed recovery attacks, or stronger optimization-based attackers. The claim of low recoverability is therefore only weakly supported.

The recoverability experiments appear circular or underspecified: supervised bit-recovery classifiers require labels for the bucket bits, which a keyless analyst would not have in the stated threat model. It is unclear what data the defender is assumed to possess and why failure of XGBoost/MLP baselines implies meaningful unrecoverability.

Attack effectiveness is modest in absolute terms and mixed across settings. Several headline improvements are relative gains from low baselines, e.g. 17% to 30%, 24% to 43%, and 9% to 19% exact recovery; many configurations still fail more often than they succeed, and some embedding variants underperform the ASCII+parity baseline.

The detection contribution is not established as a deployable detector. The bit-probe setting assumes the defender knows the encoding scheme, contradicting the low-recoverability premise, while the embedding-regression setting uses labeled secrets and hidden states from only 1,000 samples and five generic prompts. The paper reports probe separability but does not give a realistic detection protocol, false-positive calibration against benign fine-tuned models, or robustness to adaptive attackers.

The theoretical KL/perplexity results do not justify the strong conclusion that traditional steganalysis is insufficient. They are lower-bound/idealized arguments under restrictive assumptions, not empirical evidence that practical high-capacity covert channels remain indistinguishable from benign fine-tuning. No matched benign fine-tuning baselines are provided for the claimed “normal fine-tuning ranges.”

The text quality evaluation is too small and weakly reported: coherence/stability use only 10 prompts, KL uses 20 prompts, and the paper mainly relies on plots without strong statistical comparison to benign fine-tunes. This is inadequate for claims about imperceptibility or deployability.

Reproducibility is incomplete for a dual-use systems paper. Hyperparameters are listed, but the attack code is not promised for release, detection code is only future-tense, and key implementation details such as data generation, constrained decoding, seed search, and classifier training are not sufficient to independently validate the results.

The paper’s presentation overstates several findings. Terms such as “unrecoverable,” “detect,” and “large payloads” are used more strongly than the evidence warrants, and the conclusion does not adequately temper claims given low exact-match rates, limited detector validation, and the strong access assumptions.

Ethically, the paper presents improved covert exfiltration methods but gives only a high-level responsible-disclosure statement. The mitigation plan is thin relative to the dual-use risk, especially since the defensive method requires white-box hidden-state access and may not help many realistic deployments.

strengths: The paper tackles an important and timely security problem: malicious fine-tuning can create covert exfiltration channels even when deployment limits network access. The threat model and attack/defense framing are mostly clear.

The recoverability distinction is useful. Separating token-to-bucket recoverability from bucket-to-secret recoverability clarifies why prior ASCII/parity schemes are easy to reverse-engineer, and gives a concrete diagnostic beyond standard fluency or KL-based steganalysis.

The embedding-hyperplane bucketing idea is simple, plausible, and empirically useful. Across Llama-8B, Ministral-8B, and Llama-70B settings, the proposed variants often improve exact secret recovery while reducing classifier-based recoverability relative to ASCII+parity.

The evaluation is broader than a minimal proof of concept: it includes multiple model families, LoRA versus full fine-tuning, Wiki/TrojanStego-style data, OOD prompt tests, text-quality metrics, recoverability probes, and internal linear-probe detection.

The detection-side result is interesting: late-layer activations appear to carry stronger secret information in steganographically fine-tuned models than in base models, including in a masked control where output-side decoding is intentionally blocked.
The paper is generally readable and includes useful appendices with notation, proof sketches, classifier details, training hyperparameters, probe details, and a dual-use impact statement.
weaknesses: The central security claim of low recoverability is only evaluated against a narrow set of classifiers. XGBoost/MLP probes over token IDs or embeddings are a weak proxy for a determined defender who can query the model, exploit known plaintext prompts, search seeds, fit bucket partitions, or use stronger representation/model-extraction attacks. The paper cites seed recovery concerns but does not seriously evaluate them.

The embedding-bucketing construction relies on a single random hyperplane seed in the reported setup, and Appendix D states the seed is fixed at 42. This raises concerns about robustness: results may depend on lucky hyperplanes, and no analysis is given over seed choices, bucket balance beyond medianing, or adversarial recovery across seeds.

The exact-match attack success rates remain modest in key realistic settings. For example, several LoRA settings are around 20-40%, and the Llama-70B result improves from 9% to 19%. These are meaningful relative gains but still leave ambiguity about practical exfiltration reliability, especially without repetition/error-correction analysis or realistic deployment workflows.

The detection experiments do not yet establish a deployable detector. They assume white-box hidden-state access and use prompts containing known plaintext secrets to train probes. The gray-box embedding regression is promising, but the paper does not show robust model-level detection rates, false-positive rates across benign fine-tunes, or resilience to an adaptive attacker trained to suppress probe signals.

The theoretical KL/perplexity section is suggestive but overclaimed. Lower bounds and toy assumptions about next-token probabilities do not by themselves show that large payloads can actually be hidden with low distributional shift in realistic generation while preserving utility, semantics, and trainability.

The text-quality evidence is thin. Coherence/stability are computed on very small prompt counts, perplexity/KL are not convincingly calibrated against comparable benign fine-tunes, and there is no human evaluation or task-utility evaluation. This weakens claims that the outputs are unobtrusive enough for realistic covert exfiltration.

The threat model could be sharper. The defender is said to inspect and query the model but lack the key; however, the recoverability and detection evaluations make different assumptions about access to hidden states, known encodings, and labeled secrets. The paper would benefit from explicitly mapping each experiment to a defender capability tier.

Originality is moderate rather than high: random hyperplane partitioning in embedding space is closely related to semantic watermarking and hashing-style constructions, and linear probes are a standard interpretability tool. The contribution is useful mainly in combining these ideas for fine-tuning-based LLM steganography rather than introducing a fundamentally new method.

Reproducibility is partially addressed through hyperparameters and planned code release, but full reproducibility would require release of generated datasets, exact seeds for all hyperplanes and splits, decoding constraints, and enough detail to reproduce the expensive fine-tuning runs. The attack code is not promised for open release due to dual-use concerns, which is understandable but limits reproducibility.

strengths: The paper studies an important and timely dual-use problem: covert exfiltration through fine-tuned LLMs, and it clearly distinguishes attack-side recoverability from detection-side evidence. This framing is useful and more nuanced than simply measuring whether a stego channel works.

The proposed embedding-hyperplane bucketing idea is simple, plausible, and empirically improves exact secret recovery in several settings while reducing recoverability under the authors' classifier-based tests. The experiments cover multiple models, full vs. LoRA tuning, Wiki/TrojanStego/mixed-motive data, OOD prompt transfer, temperature robustness, retokenization effects, and capability degradation.

The paper includes a candid limitations section and an impact statement. It acknowledges hidden-state access assumptions, restricted secret lengths, black-box detection gaps, symbolic-task degradation, and dual-use concerns.

Presentation is generally clear, with useful tables and appendices giving training details, classifier details, and probe setup. The work is easy to follow despite combining attack construction, empirical evaluation, and detection.
weaknesses: The central claim of 'low recoverability' is only supported against a narrow set of learned classifiers. Rbucket and Rsecret are operationalized with XGBoost/MLPs on token IDs or embeddings, but this does not convincingly model a capable defender who knows the algorithm, can optimize over hyperplane seeds, exploit known plaintext/secret formats, use many more samples, or perform cryptanalytic/search attacks. Thus the main security claim is under-supported.

The detection method is not yet a realistic detector. The probes are trained with labels for the secret that is explicitly present in the prompt, and compare fine-tuned models to base models; in practice a defender may not have labeled secret-output pairs, may not know which prompts contain secrets, and may not have a clean base model or matched benign fine-tunes. The method demonstrates enhanced linear accessibility of prompt secrets after stego fine-tuning, but not a deployable detection pipeline with controlled false positives across ordinary fine-tuned models.

Several empirical results are much weaker than the abstract suggests. Exact-match recovery remains modest in many important cases, e.g. many LoRA settings are in the 20-45% range and OOD transfer can collapse to near zero depending on the train/eval prompt mismatch. The paper sometimes emphasizes relative gains from low baselines rather than absolute reliability.

The theoretical KL/perplexity arguments do not establish that traditional steganalysis is ineffective in the studied setting. They are lower-bound/idealized constructions under simplified assumptions about bucket targets and argmax promotion, but they do not rule out practical detectors using richer distributional, semantic, calibration, or fine-tune comparison signals.

Text quality and capability evaluation are too limited to support strong deployment plausibility. Coherence/stability are computed on very small prompt counts, the metrics are weak proxies for suspicious behavior, and the capability drops are often large, especially for full fine-tuning and Ministral. Mixed-motive training helps but does not fully close this concern.

The strongest detection figures rely on visual plots without enough tabulated numeric detail, statistical testing, or benign fine-tuning controls. It is unclear whether the observed probe gaps are specific to steganographic fine-tuning rather than generic memorization of prompt fields, instruction-template artifacts, or distribution shift induced by any secret-conditioned objective.

Reproducibility is partial. The appendices contain useful hyperparameters, but the impact statement says only detection code will be released while attack code will be coordinated with providers. For a paper whose core contributions include attack construction and recoverability evaluation, this limits independent verification.

The paper has some presentation and rigor issues: terminology alternates between detection, recovery, and reverse engineering; some claims are stronger than the evidence warrants; there are typos and awkward phrasing; and Figure 2/5 convey important conclusions without enough precise numerical reporting.

strengths: The paper studies an important dual-use security problem: whether fine-tuned LLMs can covertly exfiltrate prompt-borne secrets, and how defenders might detect such behavior.

The attack-side idea of replacing token-ID parity with seed-dependent embedding-space hyperplane bucketing is simple, plausible, and empirically reduces recoverability under the authors' classifier-based tests.

The manuscript evaluates several model/training settings, including Llama-8B, Ministral-8B, and a 70B LoRA setting, and includes in-distribution, OOD prompt, text-quality, capability, mixed-motive, temperature, and retokenization analyses.

The paper contains an explicit impact statement and limitations section. It appropriately acknowledges dual-use risks, hidden-state access assumptions for detection, degradation on symbolic tasks, limited payload sizes, and scaling issues for the embedding-based character encoder.
weaknesses: The central claims are substantially stronger than the evidence. Absolute exact-match rates remain low in many key settings: e.g. 17->30%, 24->43%, and 9->19% are presented as large relative gains, but these are unreliable exfiltration channels in absolute terms. Several configurations underperform the ASCII+Parity baseline, especially for embedding encoding and some full-finetuning settings.

The main methodological novelty is limited. The best-performing variant is often ASCII+Embedding, meaning the useful contribution is mainly replacing parity bucketing with random hyperplane bucketing. This is close in spirit to existing watermarking/steganographic partitioning ideas, and the embedding-based secret encoder itself appears weak, sometimes worse than ASCII, and explicitly scales poorly beyond small alphabets.

The recoverability metric is not fully convincing as a security measure. Rbucket and Rsecret are estimated with supervised classifiers that require labels for bits/secrets, whereas the stated defender is keyless. This makes the metric useful as a diagnostic but not a realistic operational notion of reverse engineering. The paper does not analyze stronger seed-recovery, adaptive, or cryptanalytic baselines in enough depth.

The detection evidence is hard to interpret. Linear probes are trained with labeled secrets on prompts that explicitly contain the secret string. This raises the concern that probes exploit secret information already present in the prompt/context or distributional artifacts of fine-tuning, rather than detecting a robust steganographic mechanism. The method also assumes white-/gray-box hidden-state access and supervised labeled probe data, limiting its practical defense value.

The theoretical KL/perplexity section overclaims. The bounds describe minimum possible distribution shift under idealized assumptions and do not establish that trained models can actually hide large payloads while remaining undetectable. The discussion jumps from lower bounds and toy probability assumptions to broad claims that traditional steganalysis is insufficient, without a strong empirical output-only detector comparison.

Capability and utility costs are serious. Table 3 shows large drops on standard benchmarks for single-objective steganographic fine-tuning, often around 10-30 percentage points. Mixed-motive training mitigates this for some LoRA cases but does not eliminate the concern, especially for full fine-tuning and Ministral.

The OOD generalization story is mixed. Wiki-trained full models often fail on TrojanStego/helpful-style prompts, and TrojanStego-trained models largely fail on Wiki prompts. This weakens the claim that the attack generalizes broadly across realistic deployment prompts.

Reproducibility is incomplete. The appendices provide many details, but the impact statement says only detection code will be released and attack code will be coordinated with providers. Critical details such as exact generated datasets, selected seeds beyond the bucketing seed, decoding/generation settings, model versions, and full evaluation scripts are needed for reliable reproduction.

Presentation needs tightening. Some sections contain typos and awkward phrasing, figures are dense, and important distinctions among encoding, bucketing, payload recovery, attack success, and detection are sometimes blurred. The paper repeatedly emphasizes relative gains and 'state-of-the-art' recovery without sufficiently foregrounding low absolute reliability and capability degradation.

Overall, the paper has a relevant problem and some useful experiments, but the contribution is incremental, the detection and theory are not strong enough to support the broad conclusions, and the empirical results are too mixed for acceptance in the main track.

strengths: The paper addresses an important and timely security problem: training-time LLM steganography under restricted egress, and it usefully separates attack-side payload recoverability from detectability. The distinction between recovering the payload and merely detecting abnormal distributional shift is conceptually valuable.

The embedding-space hyperplane construction is simple, well motivated, and empirically improves over the TrojanStego-style ASCII+parity baseline in many settings, especially LoRA models and the 70B setting. The recoverability analysis also clearly shows why parity bucketing is a brittle baseline.

The evaluation is broader than many papers in this area: multiple model families, LoRA and full fine-tuning, Wiki/TrojanStego/mixed-motive data, OOD prompt evaluation, capability degradation, retokenization robustness, temperature robustness, and several text-quality metrics.

The detection-side experiments are a useful contribution. The late-layer linear-probe gaps, including in mixed-motive and XOR-masked controls, suggest that fine-tuning-based steganography may leave internal signatures even when output-side recovery is hard.

The limitations and impact sections are unusually candid. The authors acknowledge limited payload size, dependence on trigger/prompt observability, degradation on symbolic tasks, scaling issues for embedding-based character codes, and the hidden-state access requirement for their strongest detector.
weaknesses: The central security notion of low recoverability is not yet fully convincing. The empirical Rbucket/Rsecret estimates depend on a small set of supervised classifiers and do not approximate a strong adaptive defender. In particular, the defender's access to chosen prompts, known secrets, labels, or model embeddings is not cleanly formalized, so the reported low recoverability may partly reflect the chosen attack model for the classifier rather than true resistance to reverse engineering.

Attack reliability remains moderate in absolute terms. Many headline improvements are large in relative terms but exact-match rates are often only 20-50%, with 70B reaching 19% in the highlighted setting. Since the paper frames this as covert exfiltration, the practical implications of such failure rates, retransmission, error correction, and larger or realistic secrets are underdeveloped.

The detection method is better described as supervised probing/recovery under white-box or gray-box access than as a deployable detector. It requires hidden states and labeled/probed data, and the paper does not sufficiently evaluate false positives on benign fine-tunes that also condition generation on prompt secrets, keys, IDs, or other structured prompt variables.

The claim that standard steganalysis is insufficient is somewhat overextended. The KL/perplexity bounds are interesting but rely on idealized argmax-promotion assumptions and do not by themselves establish that realistic trained models can hide large payloads while remaining indistinguishable from normal fine-tuning. Empirical distributional-shift comparisons are limited and could use stronger benign fine-tuning controls.

Some experimental choices make interpretation difficult: the base model already receives the plaintext secret in the prompt, base probes achieve nontrivial accuracy, and the paper does not fully disentangle secret representation caused by ordinary prompt processing from steganographic encoding behavior. More controls with non-steganographic secret-conditioned training would strengthen the mechanistic claims.

Reproducibility is only partial. The paper provides many hyperparameters and classifier details, but the impact statement says only detection code will be released while attack code will be coordinated with providers. That is ethically understandable, but it limits independent verification of the main attack-side results.
